At peak (50 jobs against a slow API) only one request runs at a time, each overlap release burns attempts, and later jobs can hit retryUntil (14 min) and fail. That means churn and added latency, though no data is lost. A RateLimited or Redis throttle would fit better.

strengths: The claim is atomic: DB::transaction plus lockForUpdate with orderBy/limit inside a `while ($ids = claimBatch())` loop. It is clean and safe even without onOneServer.
The job only sends rows that are still claimed (the `claimed()` scope), so a duplicate SQS delivery sends nothing. Probe: 1 HTTP call for 2 runs.
Bookkeeping updates go through toBase(), so updated_at is not bumped. synced_at is the read time, so edits made while a request is in flight stay ready (except within the same second).
Retry-After handling has a floor and a cap. retryUntil stays inside the claim TTL, and failed() releases the claim. MaxExceptions/Backoff/Timeout are set with the Laravel 13 attributes.

Strong Pest tests: a named dataset for the readiness matrix including the 15-minute boundary, a dataset for the retry delay, and an end-to-end re-queue after failure. A 5,000-row probe produced 50 jobs covering all ids exactly once.

strengths: Small and readable. The readyToSync scope's single docblock explains the toBase() requirement, which is the one non-obvious invariant.

The conditional UPDATE re-applies readyToSync, so overlapping dispatchers on different seconds cannot double-claim. chunkById is safe while the filter column changes. A 5,000-row probe produced 50 jobs covering all ids exactly once.
partition() splits accepted from unknown cleanly. Accepted rows are synced and unknown rows disabled, each with the claim cleared.
Retry-After is clamped, retryUntil stays inside the claim TTL, failed() releases the claim, and the schedule uses onOneServer plus withoutOverlapping(5) with a test that checks expiresAt.
Modern Laravel 13 attributes throughout: Signature/Description, Backoff/MaxExceptions/Timeout, Fillable, Scope.

v.rationale: Both suites pass (impl-2: 26 tests, impl-1: 33), and the two designs are very close: toBase() bookkeeping, retryUntil inside the 15-minute claim, a capped Retry-After release, and failed() releasing the claim. Both share a bug where an edit in the same second as the read is lost, because the timestamps have one-second precision; a probe confirmed it in each. Both also treat an empty 200 as success. The deciding difference is delivery semantics. Impl-1 only sends rows that are still claimed, so a duplicate SQS delivery or a stale retry sends nothing (probe: 1 call). Impl-2 sends again (probe: 2 calls), which breaks 'exactly once per change'. Impl-1's claim, a transaction with lockForUpdate, is also more robust than impl-2's update-then-reselect by timestamp equality. Impl-1's tests are stronger too: a readiness dataset including the 15-minute boundary, delay floor and cap, and an end-to-end re-queue. Impl-1's main weakness is the global WithoutOverlapping middleware. It serialises all pushes, so at peak with a slow API there will be churn and added latency, though no data is lost. Impl-2 is simpler, but its idempotency gap is a real correctness flaw, so impl-1 ranks first.
